individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic action paradigm that decouples action execution from task-specific conditioning for bimanual manipulation. It proposes ATARA, an automated RL-based data collection method that generates 610k image-action pairs in about 10 hours, and AnyPos, an inverse dynamics model with arm-decoupled estimation and a direction-aware decoder. The pipeline is evaluated on action prediction accuracy, real-world video replay, and deployment with a video generation model, reporting improvements over a ResNet+MLP baseline and human-collected data.
Strengths: ATARA provides a scalable and automated alternative to human teleoperation, collecting 610k task-agnostic image-action pairs in 10 hours and reporting a 30x speedup.

AnyPos introduces sensible architectural components (arm-decoupled estimation via flood-fill segmentation, multi-scale dilated convolutions, deformable convolutions, and angle-sensitive pooling) that improve prediction accuracy from 5.83% to 57.13% on the benchmark.

The real-world replay results show a 92.59% success rate, which is substantially higher than the 59.26% achieved with a model trained on human-collected data, suggesting practical benefit from task-agnostic data.
The integration with a video generation model demonstrates a potential path toward language-conditioned manipulation without explicit task-specific action labels.
Weaknesses: The theoretical decomposition in Eq. (4) assumes p(a_i | x_i) is task-agnostic and that the observed image uniquely determines the joint configuration, but multiple joint states can yield the same image due to occlusion or visual aliasing; this assumption is not justified.

The comparison with prior IDM methods is weak: the only strong baseline is ResNet+MLP, which is not representative of the actual IDMs used in UniPi, SuSIE, RoboDreamer, or UniSim. No direct comparisons with these methods are performed.

The human-data comparison is confounded by dataset size: ATARA has 610k pairs while the human-collected dataset has only 33k, so the higher replay success of AnyPos-ATARA may be due to more data rather than the task-agnostic paradigm.

The real-world replay evaluation uses only 10 tasks with a single trial each, making the success rates statistically fragile. The accuracy threshold of 0.06 is chosen empirically without sensitivity analysis.
The video-generation deployment experiments are qualitative only; there are no quantitative success rates, number of trials, or details about Vidu finetuning, making it hard to assess robustness.

The paper does not explain how the RL-based ATARA policy is transferred from simulation to the real robot, nor what safety measures are in place during autonomous random action collection, which is a significant practical concern.
Clarity is hurt by multiple typos and notation issues (e.g., '30×30×30×', 'AnyPos-ATATA', ill-defined multiple integrals) and by missing details in the main text that are deferred to appendices.
Questions: How was the RL policy from ATARA deployed to collect the 610k real-robot trajectories? What safety constraints, stop conditions, or collision checks were used during autonomous random exploration?

In the decomposition p(a|x,l)=∫p(x'|x,l)p(a|x')dx', why is p(a|x') task-agnostic and not dependent on the language instruction? How does AnyPos handle the fact that many joint configurations can produce the same image?

What exactly does 'test accuracy' measure? Is a prediction considered accurate only if all 14 joints are within the thresholds, and how sensitive are the downstream success rates to the chosen 0.06 threshold?
For the real-world replay benchmark, what is the exact success metric? Are reported success rates per full task or per sub-action, and how many trials were conducted per task?
In the video-generation deployment, what was the success rate and how many trials were run? What video generation model was used besides mentioning Vidu 2.0, and how was it finetuned?
Why were no ablations of the individual DAD components (dilated convolution, deformable convolution, angle-sensitive pooling) reported? What is the contribution of each?
Would the method work with different camera placements, backgrounds, or robot embodiments? How dependent is the arm-decoupled segmentation on the fixed workspace and uniform black arms?
Limitations: Only evaluated on one dual-arm robot platform with fixed camera views; no cross-embodiment or multi-camera generalization experiments.
The study relies on a small evaluation set (2.5k test pairs, 10 replay tasks), and replay tasks are single-trial, limiting statistical confidence.
The ATARA data collection requires a simulator-trained RL policy and known robot URDF; the paper does not detail sim-to-real transfer or safety precautions for autonomous real-robot data collection.
AnyPos predicts joint positions only, not velocities, torques, or closed-loop feedback, which may limit applicability to highly dynamic or contact-rich tasks.
The video-generation integration is demonstrated only qualitatively, with no quantitative success rates or robustness analysis under distribution shift.

The paper mentions background generalization as future work but does not test the model under significant visual domain shifts aside from minor color jitter and background randomization during training.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes a task-agnostic action paradigm to address the high cost of robot data collection. It introduces ATARA, an RL-based automated data collection method that generates random trajectories covering the robot workspace, and AnyPos, an inverse dynamics model with arm-decoupled estimation and a direction-aware decoder to predict joint positions from images. The system is evaluated on a real robot (Mobile ALOHA) with 610k image-action pairs collected automatically, achieving 57.13% test accuracy and 92.59% success rate on video replay, along with a claimed 30x data collection speedup over human teleoperation. The paper also demonstrates integration with a video generation model for real-world tasks.
Strengths: The idea of automated task-agnostic data collection (ATARA) is a creative and practical solution to the high cost of human demonstrations, using RL in simulation to cover the workspace efficiently.
The decomposition of policy learning into task-specific video generation and task-agnostic inverse dynamics is a principled direction that could improve scalability and reusability of robot data.
Arm-decoupled estimation and the Direction-Aware Decoder are sensible architectural improvements that provide clear quantitative gains over simpler baselines.
The paper includes real robot experiments, detailed implementation descriptions, and hardware specifications, which aids reproducibility.
The empirical results show that automated random data can surpass human-collected data in terms of downstream success rate, which is an interesting and valuable finding.
Weaknesses: The 'real-world replay' evaluation is open-loop: the model is given frames from a human demonstration and its per-frame action predictions are executed after resetting the environment. This does not test closed-loop policy generalization, reactivity, or robustness, so the reported 92.59% success rate is not a standard measure of policy performance.

The accuracy claims are misleading: the '51% improvement' is actually a 51.3 percentage-point increase (from 5.83% to 57.13%), not a 51% relative improvement; similarly, '30–40% higher success rates' appears to be percentage points.

The comparison with human-collected data is confounded by dataset size (610k vs 33k) and training iterations; the human-trained model has higher test accuracy (57.78%) but lower replay success (59.26%), which is not adequately explained.

The method is evaluated on a single robot platform and workspace; generalization to other embodiments, camera configurations, or cluttered environments is not demonstrated despite claims of embodiment-aware reusability.

The mathematical decomposition in Eq. (4) ignores the fact that actions affect future observations, and the factorized inverse model p(a_i | x_i) may not be identifiable from images alone in partially observed settings.
No comparison with state-of-the-art IDM or VLA models (e.g., Seer, VPP, Gen2Act, RDT, OpenVLA) is provided; the baselines are limited to ResNet+MLP and DINOv2+MLP.
The real-world deployment with video generation lacks quantitative success rates; only qualitative examples are shown, making it unclear how reliable the integrated system is.
Questions: How is the replay success rate computed? How many trials per task, and what is the variance? The appendix says real-world implementations are typically limited to a single trial; if so, the 92.59% figure is based on very few trials.

What exactly does 'Test Acc.' measure? Is it the fraction of samples where all 14 joint predictions are within the thresholds (0.06 for arm joints, 0.5 for grippers), or a per-joint metric? Please clarify.
How are the 0.06 and 0.5 thresholds derived? How robust is the accuracy metric to these thresholds?
In ATARA, how are trajectories generated? Do you sample target points and execute straight-line motions in joint space to the predicted configurations? How are intermediate images captured?

What data was used to finetune the Vidu 2.0 video generation model? If it was finetuned on task-specific human demonstrations, then the overall system still depends on task-specific data, undermining the claim of task-agnostic learning.
Can you provide quantitative success rates for the real-world deployment with video generation? The paper only shows example tasks without success rates or number of trials.
How does AnyPos handle occlusions or objects that obscure the arms? The flood-fill segmentation fails when arms overlap and falls back to a bounding box heuristic—how does this affect accuracy?
How is the 30x data collection speedup measured? Does it include the time to set up and run simulation, or only robot data collection time?
Limitations: The replay evaluation is open-loop and does not reflect closed-loop policy performance; this is a major limitation not disclosed in the main text.

The overall framework still relies on a task-specific video generation model (Vidu), which likely requires task-specific training data; the claim of a 'task-agnostic action paradigm' is therefore only partially realized.
The arm-decoupling segmentation heuristic is brittle and relies on the arms being black and pedestal joints visible; it may not generalize to other robots or environments.

The action prediction accuracy is only 57% even though the paper claims high precision; this suggests many actions are not precisely predicted, and success depends on the forgiving nature of many manipulation steps, which is not analyzed.
The experiments are limited to a single robot and do not test zero-shot transfer to different morphologies or camera angles, despite the claim of embodiment-aware reusability.
The paper does not discuss the computational cost of the video generation model or its real-time usability.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes a task-agnostic action paradigm for robot manipulation, decoupling action execution from task-specific conditioning. It introduces ATARA, an RL-based automated data collection pipeline that generates random, collision-free joint configurations, and AnyPos, an inverse dynamics model with arm-decoupled estimation and a direction-aware decoder. Experiments on a dual-arm ALOHA robot show improved action prediction accuracy and real-world replay success compared to baselines, and the model is combined with a video generation model for task execution.
Strengths: The task-agnostic data collection paradigm is timely and addresses a real bottleneck: the high cost of task-specific demonstrations.
ATARA enables 30x faster data collection without human labor, and the authors provide both accuracy and real-robot replay comparisons against human-collected data.
The AnyPos architecture ablations show clear gains from arm decoupling and the DAD decoder, and the paper identifies a practical issue (cross-arm interference) with attention-map evidence.
Real-robot replay on 10 long-horizon bimanual tasks is a nontrivial evaluation that demonstrates the potential of the approach.
Weaknesses: The theoretical decomposition in Eq. (2)-(4) is not rigorously justified; it assumes actions are conditionally independent of the initial observation and language given future images, and that joint positions are fully recoverable from a single image, which is often violated in practice.

Critical experimental details are missing: how the PPO policy trained in simulation is transferred to the real robot for ATARA collection, the exact accuracy metric (per-sample vs per-dimension), and quantitative success rates for the generated-video deployment.

The replay evaluation is based on open-loop execution of ground-truth videos; it does not measure closed-loop performance under feedback, and the 92.59% success rate seems inconsistent with 57% joint accuracy unless the metric is permissive or only a few timesteps matter.

The comparison with prior IDMs is limited to a simple ResNet+MLP baseline; no quantitative comparison with recently proposed IDMs or VLA models is included, so the claimed state-of-the-art is not established.

The approach relies on heuristic, robot-specific components (flood-fill arm segmentation, fixed workspace partition) and a single robot morphology, so the claimed generality to other embodiments is unsupported.
The generated-video deployment is only demonstrated qualitatively; no success-rate statistics are reported, and the video generation model details are minimal.
Questions: How is the RL policy trained in simulation transferred to the real robot for ATARA data collection? What is the sim-to-real gap and its impact on workspace coverage?
What exactly is the test accuracy metric in Table 1? Is it the percentage of samples where all 14 dimensions are within threshold, or per-dimension accuracy?
Why does AnyPos-Human (trained on human data) have similar test accuracy but much lower replay success than AnyPos-ATARA? Could this be due to evaluation protocol or overfitting?
What are the quantitative success rates for the real-world deployment with Vidu-generated videos? How many tasks and trials were run, and what criteria define success?
How sensitive is the flood-fill arm segmentation to background changes, arm color, occlusion, or different camera viewpoints? Is the split line manually tuned per setup?
Could the DAD improvement be attributed simply to increased model capacity? Is there an ablation isolating each DAD component (dilated conv, deformable conv, angle-sensitive pooling)?
How does ATARA ensure behavioral coverage of manipulation-relevant states, especially contact-rich or pre-grasp configurations, beyond joint-space distributions shown in Fig. 7?
Does the IDM require camera calibration or known extrinsics, and how would it generalize to different camera placements or robot embodiments?
Limitations: Limited to a specific dual-arm ALOHA robot; no evidence of generalization to other embodiments or camera setups.
Arm-decoupled segmentation is heuristic and depends on uniform arm color and stable pedestal; occlusions or different backgrounds may break it.
The IDM is trained on random motor babbling, which may not cover contact-rich or task-relevant states; the paper does not analyze coverage of high-precision pre-grasp poses.
Real-world deployment with a video generation model is not quantitatively evaluated, so the end-to-end claims are anecdotal.
The theoretical framework assumes fully observable joint positions from images and ignores partial observability, which may limit applicability.
No analysis of failure cases or sensitivity to reset errors in the replay experiments.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic action paradigm that decouples action execution from task-specific conditioning, aiming to reduce the cost and increase the scalability of robotic data collection. It proposes ATARA, an RL-based pipeline for automated collection of random task-agnostic trajectories (610k image-action pairs collected in ~10 hours, about 30x faster than human teleoperation), and AnyPos, an inverse dynamics model that predicts joint positions from images using Arm-Decoupled Estimation and a Direction-Aware Decoder (DAD). The method is evaluated on action prediction accuracy, real-world replay from ground-truth videos, and deployment with a video generation model. Experiments report 57.13% test accuracy (vs 5.83% baseline), 92.59% real-world replay success, and successful execution of tasks such as lifting, picking/placing, and clicking with generated videos.
Strengths: Addresses an important problem: the high cost and low scalability of task-specific demonstration data for robotic manipulation.
ATARA provides a practical, automated pipeline that collects large volumes of diverse action data without human labeling, with a claimed ~30x speedup over teleoperation.
The combination of arm-decoupled estimation and DAD yields substantial accuracy improvements over simple ResNet/MLP baselines (5.83% to 57.13%).
Includes real-world validation via video replay and deployment with a video generation model, which goes beyond offline accuracy metrics.
The analysis of coverage and the comparison with human-collected data are useful steps toward understanding the value of task-agnostic data.
Weaknesses: The mathematical derivation is sloppy and contains notational errors: Eq. (4) uses x0 instead of x_T, and Eq. (3) omits the p(a|x) term that appeared in Eq. (2) while silently introducing conditional independence assumptions that are not stated or justified.

The abstract and introduction mention a 'video-conditioned action validation module', but no such learned module is introduced; the experiments only use ground-truth videos for replay evaluation, which is a protocol, not a module.

There is a confusing mismatch between action prediction accuracy (57.13%) and replay success (92.59%). The claim that 'few critical actions need high precision' is not supported by per-step or per-task breakdowns, making it unclear why the 0.06 threshold is meaningful and how 43% of predictions can be wrong yet tasks still succeed.
Table 3 contains a typo 'AnyPos-ATATA' and the text interchangeably uses 'ATATA' and 'ATARA', undermining clarity. Several figure references are broken/redacted, making the paper difficult to follow.

ATARA is described as 'self-supervised', but it relies on PPO in simulation, which is not self-supervised learning; the novelty over simple random joint-space sampling is not demonstrated with ablations—only a qualitative statement.

The comparison with human data is confounded: the human dataset is much smaller (33k vs 610k) and trained for fewer iterations, so the higher replay success of AnyPos-ATARA could be due to data volume rather than task-agnostic coverage, and this is not analyzed.
No multi-embodiment experiments are provided despite the 'embodiment-aware reusability' claim; all results are on a single robot with a fixed camera setup.
Real-world replay experiments appear to be single-trial per task, with no variance or statistical significance reported; the paper does not report per-stage success rates or error tolerance analysis.

The proposed DAD is a generic composition of dilated convolutions, deformable convolutions, and rotation pooling; no ablations isolate the contribution of each component, and the DAD only adds ~20% over a simpler MLP head.
Questions: In Eq. (4), should x0 be x_T? Can the authors provide a rigorous derivation of the decomposition with all independence assumptions explicitly stated?

How exactly is the 92.59% replay success rate computed when action prediction accuracy is only 57.13%? Is every predicted action executed, or are some actions filtered? What is the success rate per individual manipulation step, and how many predicted actions exceed the 0.06 threshold?
What is the 'video-conditioned action validation module' mentioned in the abstract? Is it a trained network or just the replay-based evaluation protocol?

Given that AnyPos trained on ATARA achieves similar test accuracy to AnyPos trained on human data (57.13% vs 57.78%) but much higher replay success (92.59% vs 59.26%), how do the authors rule out that this result is due to dataset size or training duration rather than the task-agnostic nature of the data?

What ablations compare ATARA's RL-based workspace coverage against naive random joint-space sampling or uniform end-effector sampling without PPO? Can the authors quantify the contribution of orientation augmentation and the boundary plane to data diversity and final performance?
How is safety ensured during ATARA data collection? Is collision checking performed, or is the virtual boundary plane the only collision-avoidance mechanism?
Would AnyPos generalize to other embodiments (e.g., different arm kinematics) without retraining the segmentation and decoupling strategy?
What is the variance in success rates across repeated replay trials? The paper reports a single trial per task; are the differences in Table 3 statistically significant?
Limitations: All experiments are conducted on a single dual-arm robot (Mobile ALOHA-like) with a fixed workspace and camera configuration; no evidence is provided for cross-embodiment generalization.
The ATARA data collection is performed in simulation with PPO, which may introduce sim-to-real gaps; the paper does not report any sim-to-real transfer analysis.
The replay evaluation is limited to 10 tasks with single trials, so the reported success rates may have high variance and may not be reliable.
The method does not address dynamic scenes, articulated objects, or tasks requiring fine force control; the action space is limited to joint positions with no velocity or torque.
The claimed 30x speedup assumes the PPO training time is negligible or not counted; the paper does not report the time spent training the RL policy for ATARA.
The paper lacks a detailed comparison with existing inverse dynamics models or VLA baselines on the same benchmark; only ResNet/MLP and DINOv2 variants are evaluated.

review.Summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic action paradigm that decouples action execution from task-specific conditioning, along with ATARA, an RL-based pipeline for automated collection of task-agnostic random action data, and AnyPos, an inverse dynamics model with Arm-Decoupled Estimation and a Direction-Aware Decoder (DAD). The authors claim 30x faster data collection than human teleoperation, 51% improvement in action prediction accuracy, and 30-40% higher success rates in real-world manipulation tasks. Experiments include action prediction benchmarks, real-world video replay, and deployment with a video generation model on a dual-arm Mobile ALOHA robot.
Strengths: The task-agnostic action paradigm is a useful conceptual contribution, framing action prediction as a modular combination of task-conditioned video generation and task-agnostic inverse dynamics.
ATARA enables large-scale, low-cost data collection (610k image-action pairs in ~10 hours) without human labor, and the workspace coverage is demonstrated via qpos distributions.

AnyPos's Arm-Decoupled Estimation mitigates cross-arm visual interference, yielding ~20% accuracy improvement, and the Direction-Aware Decoder contributes another ~20%, showing clear architectural benefits.

The pipeline outperforms a ResNet+MLP baseline substantially (57.13% vs 5.83% test accuracy) and achieves 92.59% real-world replay success, with qualitative demonstrations on tasks like lifting, clicking, and pick-and-place.
The paper validates the approach with real-robot experiments, including replay using ground-truth videos and deployment with generated videos, which strengthens the practical relevance.
Weaknesses: The abstract mentions a 'video-conditioned action validation module,' but the paper only describes replay-based validation; this module is not separately defined or evaluated, creating a mismatch.

The reported '51% improvement' and '30-40% higher success rates' are ambiguous: the accuracy gain appears to be ~51 absolute percentage points (5.83% to 57.13%), not 51% relative; success-rate improvements also mix absolute and relative numbers.

Real-world replay results are based on a single trial for each of 10 tasks (27 steps total), so the reported success rates (92.59%, 59.26%, etc.) have no variance or confidence intervals and may not be statistically reliable.

ATARA requires a pretrained RL policy in simulation to map end-effector positions to joint positions; the training time and compute for this PPO policy are not reported, understating the total cost compared to human data collection.

The inverse dynamics model predicts joint positions from a single image, which is more akin to state estimation than true inverse dynamics (which typically uses consecutive frames); this simplification and its limitation for velocity/torque actions are not thoroughly discussed.

The paper lacks comparisons with other recent IDM-based manipulation approaches (e.g., SuSIE, UniPi, Seer) on the same test set, and the video-generation integration is evaluated only qualitatively, without quantitative success rates.
ATARA's collision avoidance is based on partitioning target workspace regions, but the actual joint-space paths between configurations are not collision-checked, so safety is not guaranteed.
The distribution analysis (Fig. 7) shows per-dimension coverage but not simultaneous joint co-activation, which is more relevant for realistic manipulation tasks.
Questions: What exactly is the 'video-conditioned action validation module' described in the abstract, and how does it differ from the replay-based evaluation in Section 4.3?
How is test accuracy defined? Is it the percentage of samples where all non-gripper joint errors are below 0.06 and gripper error below 0.5?
How many trials were run for each replay task, and what was the variance and failure mode distribution? The appendix mentions 'single trial,' but this needs explicit confirmation.
How long and with what resources was the PPO policy for ATARA trained? Is this compute included in the claimed 10-hour collection time?
How does AnyPos handle different robot colors, camera angles, or severe occlusions? The flood-fill segmentation relies on fixed pedestal positions and uniform black arms.

Why does AnyPos trained on ATARA data achieve nearly the same test accuracy (57.13%) as the human-data model (57.78%) but much higher replay success (92.59% vs 59.26%)? What explains this discrepancy?
Limitations: The method is tailored to a specific dual-arm robot and camera configuration; the arm-decoupling segmentation and action space may not generalize to other morphologies.
AnyPos predicts only joint positions, not velocities or torques, which limits its applicability to dynamic or compliant control tasks.
ATARA data collection still requires a known kinematic model and a simulation-trained policy, and it executes open-loop joint positions without real-time feedback.
The evaluation is limited to a single robot platform and a small set of tasks; generalization to novel objects, backgrounds, and environments is not fully demonstrated.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts in detail, though automation and labor displacement are plausible concerns.

meta_review_model.label: area_chair_meta_review

review.Summary: The paper proposes a task-agnostic action paradigm that decouples action execution from task-specific conditioning for bimanual manipulation. It introduces ATARA, an RL-based automated data collection method that generates 610k image-action pairs in about 10 hours, and AnyPos, an inverse dynamics model with arm-decoupled estimation and a direction-aware decoder. The pipeline is evaluated on action prediction accuracy, real-world video replay, and deployment with a video generation model, reporting improvements over a ResNet+MLP baseline and human-collected data.
Strengths: The task-agnostic action paradigm is a timely conceptual contribution that could reduce the high cost of task-specific robot data collection.
ATARA provides a practical, automated pipeline that collects large volumes of diverse action data without human labeling, with a claimed ~30x speedup over teleoperation.
AnyPos's arm-decoupled estimation and direction-aware decoder yield substantial accuracy improvements over simple ResNet/MLP baselines (from 5.83% to 57.13%).
The work includes real-robot validation through video replay and qualitative deployment with a video generation model, demonstrating a potential path toward language-conditioned manipulation.
The analysis of coverage and comparison with human-collected data highlight interesting questions about the value of task-agnostic data.
Weaknesses: The theoretical decomposition (Eq. 2-4) is not rigorously justified; it assumes actions are independent of language and initial observations given future images, and that joint positions are fully recoverable from a single image, which is often violated due to partial observability.

Baselines are weak: only ResNet+MLP and DINOv2 variants are compared; no direct comparison with state-of-the-art IDMs or VLA models such as UniPi, SuSIE, or OpenVLA, so claimed state-of-the-art performance is not established.

The human-data comparison is confounded by dataset size (610k vs 33k) and training iterations; it is unclear whether the higher replay success of AnyPos-ATARA comes from the task-agnostic paradigm or simply from more data.

The real-world replay evaluation is open-loop and based on a single trial per task for 10 tasks; no variance or confidence intervals are reported, and the 92.59% success rate is inconsistent with the 57.13% per-sample test accuracy without further explanation.

The video-generation deployment is only demonstrated qualitatively; no quantitative success rates, number of trials, or details about Vidu 2.0 finetuning are provided, making the robustness of the integrated system unclear.

The arm-decoupled segmentation relies on heuristic assumptions (uniform black arms, fixed pedestal positions) and may not generalize to other embodiments, camera placements, or cluttered environments.

Critical implementation details are missing, including how the PPO policy is transferred from simulation to the real robot, safety measures during autonomous data collection, and the computational cost of training the RL policy (which is excluded from the claimed 10 hours).

The paper exhibits clarity issues: typos ('AnyPos-ATATA', '30×30×30×'), broken figure references, ill-defined multiple integrals, and a mismatch between the abstract's mention of a 'video-conditioned action validation module' and the actual replay-based evaluation.
Questions: How exactly is the 92.59% replay success rate computed when action prediction accuracy is only 57.13%? Are all predicted actions executed, or are some filtered? What is the success rate per individual manipulation step, and how many predicted actions exceed the 0.06 threshold?

How was the PPO policy trained in simulation transferred to the real robot for ATARA collection? What sim-to-real gap was observed, and what safety/collision checks were used during autonomous data collection?
In Eq. (4), should x0 be x_T? Can the authors provide a rigorous derivation with all independence assumptions explicitly stated?

Why does AnyPos trained on ATARA achieve similar test accuracy (57.13%) to the human-data model (57.78%) but much higher replay success (92.59% vs 59.26%)? Could this be due to dataset size, training duration, or evaluation protocol?

What ablations compare ATARA's RL-based workspace coverage against naive random joint-space sampling? What is the contribution of each DAD component (dilated conv, deformable conv, angle-sensitive pooling)?
What were the quantitative success rates and number of trials for the video-generation deployment? How was Vidu 2.0 finetuned, and does it still require task-specific human demonstrations?
How sensitive is the flood-fill arm segmentation to background changes, arm color, occlusion, or different camera viewpoints? Is the split line manually tuned per setup?
Would AnyPos generalize to other embodiments (e.g., different arm kinematics) without retraining the segmentation and decoupling strategy?
Limitations: All experiments are conducted on a single dual-arm robot with a fixed workspace and camera configuration; no cross-embodiment or multi-camera generalization is demonstrated.
The replay evaluation is open-loop and based on a small number of tasks (10) with single trials, providing limited statistical reliability.
The method relies on a known kinematic model and a simulator-trained RL policy for ATARA; the total compute and time for training this policy are not reported.
AnyPos predicts only joint positions, not velocities, torques, or closed-loop feedback, limiting applicability to dynamic or contact-rich tasks.
The arm-decoupling segmentation is heuristic and may fail under occlusion or with different robot appearance, and the paper does not provide robustness analysis.
The paper does not thoroughly analyze failure cases or the distribution of task-agnostic data coverage for contact-rich or high-precision manipulation states.
The video-generation integration is evaluated only qualitatively, with no quantitative success rates or analysis under distribution shift.

Weaknesses: The theoretical decomposition (Eq. 2-4) is not rigorously justified; it assumes actions are independent of language and initial observations given future images, and that joint positions are fully recoverable from a single image, which is often violated due to partial observability.

Baselines are weak: only ResNet+MLP and DINOv2 variants are compared; no direct comparison with state-of-the-art IDMs or VLA models such as UniPi, SuSIE, or OpenVLA, so claimed state-of-the-art performance is not established.

The human-data comparison is confounded by dataset size (610k vs 33k) and training iterations; it is unclear whether the higher replay success of AnyPos-ATARA comes from the task-agnostic paradigm or simply from more data.

The real-world replay evaluation is open-loop and based on a single trial per task for 10 tasks; no variance or confidence intervals are reported, and the 92.59% success rate is inconsistent with the 57.13% per-sample test accuracy without further explanation.

The video-generation deployment is only demonstrated qualitatively; no quantitative success rates, number of trials, or details about Vidu 2.0 finetuning are provided, making the robustness of the integrated system unclear.

The arm-decoupled segmentation relies on heuristic assumptions (uniform black arms, fixed pedestal positions) and may not generalize to other embodiments, camera placements, or cluttered environments.

Critical implementation details are missing, including how the PPO policy is transferred from simulation to the real robot, safety measures during autonomous data collection, and the computational cost of training the RL policy (which is excluded from the claimed 10 hours).

The paper exhibits clarity issues: typos ('AnyPos-ATATA', '30×30×30×'), broken figure references, ill-defined multiple integrals, and a mismatch between the abstract's mention of a 'video-conditioned action validation module' and the actual replay-based evaluation.
Questions: How exactly is the 92.59% replay success rate computed when action prediction accuracy is only 57.13%? Are all predicted actions executed, or are some filtered? What is the success rate per individual manipulation step, and how many predicted actions exceed the 0.06 threshold?

How was the PPO policy trained in simulation transferred to the real robot for ATARA collection? What sim-to-real gap was observed, and what safety/collision checks were used during autonomous data collection?
In Eq. (4), should x0 be x_T? Can the authors provide a rigorous derivation with all independence assumptions explicitly stated?

Why does AnyPos trained on ATARA achieve similar test accuracy (57.13%) to the human-data model (57.78%) but much higher replay success (92.59% vs 59.26%)? Could this be due to dataset size, training duration, or evaluation protocol?

What ablations compare ATARA's RL-based workspace coverage against naive random joint-space sampling? What is the contribution of each DAD component (dilated conv, deformable conv, angle-sensitive pooling)?
What were the quantitative success rates and number of trials for the video-generation deployment? How was Vidu 2.0 finetuned, and does it still require task-specific human demonstrations?
How sensitive is the flood-fill arm segmentation to background changes, arm color, occlusion, or different camera viewpoints? Is the split line manually tuned per setup?
Would AnyPos generalize to other embodiments (e.g., different arm kinematics) without retraining the segmentation and decoupling strategy?
Limitations: All experiments are conducted on a single dual-arm robot with a fixed workspace and camera configuration; no cross-embodiment or multi-camera generalization is demonstrated.
The replay evaluation is open-loop and based on a small number of tasks (10) with single trials, providing limited statistical reliability.
The method relies on a known kinematic model and a simulator-trained RL policy for ATARA; the total compute and time for training this policy are not reported.
AnyPos predicts only joint positions, not velocities, torques, or closed-loop feedback, limiting applicability to dynamic or contact-rich tasks.
The arm-decoupling segmentation is heuristic and may fail under occlusion or with different robot appearance, and the paper does not provide robustness analysis.
The paper does not thoroughly analyze failure cases or the distribution of task-agnostic data coverage for contact-rich or high-precision manipulation states.
The video-generation integration is evaluated only qualitatively, with no quantitative success rates or analysis under distribution shift.
